solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Defenceless but not hurt when horse flees

indicators.note: whatever flees is no longer there, so the horse's letter leaves the word for not hurt

blocks.note: not hurt = unharmed, the word before anything leaves
horse is slang for heroin, abbreviated H; this letter goes

explanation.surface: A rider thrown clear and left defenceless, though at least unhurt, as the horse bolts away.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the H out of UNHARMED and UNARMED is left. The horse really does look like a real animal in the surface; it is only drug slang for one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone carrying no weapons has no means of defence, so the two words are straightforward synonyms.

clue.text: Bare man thrown in Welsh river

indicators.note: something thrown lands in disorder, so the letters of 'man' are scrambled
the scrambled 'man' is placed inside the name of the Welsh river

blocks.note: the Usk flows through south Wales; its letters wrap round the scrambled word
anagram fodder, three letters

explanation.surface: A naked man tossed into a river in Wales, perhaps by rowdy friends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bare' reads as an adjective describing the man, but here it is a verb meaning to reveal. The Usk is a river in south Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: To bare something is to expose or reveal it, and unmasking a person or plot exposes the truth hidden behind a disguise.

clue.text: Club in weapons collection

blocks.note: a famous football club from north London, nicknamed the Gunners
a store of arms and ammunition

explanation.walkthrough: 'Club' looks like a weapon to go in the collection, but it is the football club from north London, the Gunners.
explanation.definitionFit: Arsenal is a famous English football team, and the ordinary word means a stockpile or store of guns and munitions.

clue.text: Sail low — new angle right

blocks.note: to low is what cattle do: moo
N is the standard abbreviation for new
a rake is a slope or angle, as of a theatre stage
R = right

explanation.surface: Sailing directions: keep the sail low, then take a new angle to starboard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Low' is not an adjective about the sail but the verb for a cow's call. 'Rake' as an angle of slope is the less familiar sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A moonraker is a small light square sail set very high on a mast above the skysail on old sailing ships.

clue.text: Gloomy doctor given attention

blocks.note: DR is the usual abbreviation for doctor
to give someone your ear is to pay them attention

explanation.surface: A depressed patient's doctor finally giving the attention needed.
explanation.walkthrough: DR + EAR. The surface suggests the doctor is the gloomy one, but 'Gloomy' is only the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Drear is a literary, shortened form of dreary, meaning dull, dismal and cheerless in mood or appearance.

clue.text: Romp curtailed by French girlfriend in city

indicators.note: curtailed means having its tail cut off, so the last letter of the word for romp goes

blocks.note: a lark is a romp or bit of fun; lose its last letter
amie is French for a female friend

explanation.surface: A brief fling with a French girlfriend somewhere in a city.
explanation.walkthrough: Laramie is a city in Wyoming, familiar from Westerns; 'by' simply places one piece next to the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Laramie is a real university town in southern Wyoming, USA, so it is one example of a city.

clue.text: Official verses and unfinished scores

indicators.note: a word left unfinished is missing its ending, so the word for scores drops its final letter

blocks.note: lines of poetry are verses
scores = many (scores of people); without its last letter

explanation.surface: A match official reads out poetry while the final scores are still undecided.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scores' suggests a match result to sit beside the official, but here it means a great number, as in scores of people.
explanation.definitionFit: A linesman is the assistant referee who runs the touchline in football or tennis, one of the officials at a match.

clue.text: Almost set one, maybe two bones?

indicators.note: almost means not quite complete, so the last letter of the set is dropped

blocks.note: a radio set, missing its final letter
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A doctor has nearly finished setting a fracture and wonders whether two bones were broken.
explanation.walkthrough: RADI(O) + I. 'Set' leads toward setting a broken bone; it is the noun, as in a wireless set.
explanation.definitionFit: The radius is a forearm bone, and its Latin plural covers two of them; 'maybe' flags that any radii, not only bones, would qualify.

clue.text: Shambles in area in Sicilian city

blocks.note: a shambles is a mess
used as itself
A is a standard abbreviation for area

explanation.surface: Describes chaos in some district of a town in Sicily.
explanation.walkthrough: MESS + IN + A. The first 'in' is taken literally as letters, the second joins the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Messina is the port on the north-eastern tip of Sicily, facing the Italian mainland across the strait.

clue.text: Demented alcoholic stage concerned with final events

indicators.note: a demented mind is disordered, so the letters that follow are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: anagram fodder, fourteen letters

explanation.surface: A drunk reaching the raving phase, obsessed with how everything ends.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder is two full words, so count the letters against the fourteen squares. The surface of a drinker's last stage neatly matches the answer's sense of last things.
explanation.definitionFit: Eschatology is the branch of theology dealing with death, judgement and the end of the world, the last things of all.

clue.text: Friend across pond welcomes celebrated flyer

indicators.note: to welcome someone is to take them in, so the American friend holds the celebrated one

blocks.note: bud is American slang for a friend, the pond being the Atlantic
star as an adjective, as in a star player

explanation.surface: An American pal greets a famous pilot arriving from the other side of the Atlantic.
explanation.walkthrough: BU(STAR)D. 'Across pond' is the crossword way of saying American. The 'celebrated flyer' tempts as one unit, a famous aviator, but the definition is only the last word.
explanation.definitionFit: A bustard is a large heavy ground bird of open plains, and being a bird that can take off it counts as something that flies.

clue.text: Sweet roll with chopped dates good for diet

indicators.note: chopped fruit is cut up and jumbled, so the letters of the fruit are rearranged

blocks.note: a bun is a sweet bread roll
anagram fodder, five letters
G is the standard abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: A recipe note claiming a sticky date bun is healthy slimming food.
explanation.walkthrough: BUN + DESTA + G. 'Diet' is not about eating: it is a legislative assembly, the old name for several European parliaments.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bundestag is the German federal parliament, and diet is the traditional English word for such a national legislative assembly.

clue.text: Unstressed syllable in school was cut

indicators.note: a word that is cut has been shortened, so the past tense of be loses its end

blocks.note: SCH is a standard abbreviation for school
'was' with its final letter removed

explanation.surface: A lesson in which one weak syllable gets dropped from a word.
explanation.walkthrough: SCH + WA(S). The surface suggests a pronunciation lesson, which fits the answer's world, while 'cut' actually works on 'was'.
explanation.definitionFit: The schwa is the neutral vowel sound heard in the weak, unaccented beats of English words, like the first letter of about.

clue.text: Prepared for war theatre, MOD ordered choppers

indicators.note: things ordered are put into a new arrangement, so the letters before it are rearranged

blocks.note: anagram fodder, ten letters
choppers is slang for teeth

explanation.surface: The Ministry of Defence orders helicopters for a war theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: The MOD is the UK Ministry of Defence. 'Choppers' strongly suggests helicopters in this military surface, but it is slang for teeth, and 'war' belongs to the definition, not the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone carrying every weapon they could possibly have, fully equipped and ready for fighting.

clue.text: Female following obese man sent north

indicators.note: in a down entry, sending letters north makes them read from the bottom up

blocks.note: F is the abbreviation for following, as in page references
obese = fat
Sid, a man's name

explanation.surface: A woman trailing a fat man who is being dispatched northwards.
explanation.walkthrough: F + FAT + SID, the whole string read upwards. The distaff side of a family is the mother's side.
explanation.definitionFit: A distaff was the staff used in spinning, traditionally women's work, so the word came to mean relating to women or the maternal line.

clue.text: Maiden is deity accepting writer not well directed

indicators.note: to accept something is to take it in, so the deity takes the writer inside

blocks.note: M is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for a maiden over
used as itself
a deity is a god; its letters go round the writer
Jules Verne, the French novelist

explanation.surface: A young woman who is a goddess taking in an author who feels unwell and misled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Writer' could be almost any author; the letters available between the deity's G-O and D point to Jules Verne.
explanation.definitionFit: To misgovern is to rule or manage badly, so a country or body run poorly has been badly directed by its leaders.

clue.text: Back in first of several additional residences

blocks.note: to back a motion is to second it
in, as in 'is she in?', means at home
the opening letter of 'several'

explanation.surface: Suggests someone moving back into the first of a string of spare properties they own.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' is a verb, as in supporting a proposal at a meeting, and 'in' means at home rather than inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A second home is a holiday cottage or flat owned besides a main house, so several of them are extra places to live.

clue.text: Rocket incorporating new submarine detection system

indicators.note: to incorporate is to take into the body, so the verb for rocket holds the letter for new

blocks.note: to rocket is to soar, as prices do
N is the standard abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A new missile fitted with equipment for tracking enemy submarines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rocket' is a verb here, to shoot upward, not the missile the military surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: The system sends sound pulses through water and listens for echoes, which is how navies locate vessels hidden beneath the sea.

clue.text: Composer admits small offence to French king

indicators.note: to admit someone is to let them in, so the small offence goes inside the French king

blocks.note: roi is French for king; it wraps round the rest
S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
a sin is an offence

explanation.surface: A composer confesses a minor wrong done to a king of France.
explanation.walkthrough: Gioachino Rossini wrote The Barber of Seville and the William Tell overture. The small offence is two pieces, the size letter and the sin.
explanation.definitionFit: Rossini was the nineteenth-century Italian writer of operas, so he is one example of someone who composes music.

clue.text: Russian empress one departing Mediterranean port

indicators.note: whatever is departing leaves, so the numeral for one goes from the port's name

blocks.note: the great Egyptian port on the Mediterranean
I is the Roman numeral for one; this letter leaves

explanation.surface: A Russian empress sailing away from a port in the Mediterranean.
explanation.walkthrough: The Egyptian city founded by Alexander the Great loses its second-to-last letter. 'One departing' reads as a person leaving, but it is the numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: Alexandra Feodorovna was the wife of Nicholas II, the last tsar, and so the final empress consort of Russia.

clue.text: Anxious to enjoy a drama by Williams

annotation.answer: LIKE A CAT ON A HOT TIN ROOF

blocks.note: to enjoy something is to like it
used as itself
Tennessee Williams's 1955 play set on a Mississippi plantation

explanation.surface: Someone nervous about going to see a play by the American dramatist.
explanation.walkthrough: The play title supplies most of the letters; the verb for enjoy and the article in front turn it into the well-known simile.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone jumpy, restless and on edge, as a cat would be forced to hop about on hot metal.

clue.text: Subject of ace supporter nursing broken leg

indicators.note: a broken limb is out of shape, so the letters of the leg are rearranged
to nurse something is to hold it close, so the ace and supporter wrap round the broken leg

blocks.note: A is the card abbreviation for ace
anagram fodder, three letters
a bra is a supporting undergarment, a crossword favourite for supporter

explanation.surface: A star sports fan who cares for someone with a fractured leg becomes the talk of the town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supporter' suggests a football fan beside the ace, but it is an item of underwear. The broken leg sits between the first letter and the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Algebra is the branch of mathematics using letters for unknown numbers, and so is one example of a school subject.

clue.text: Some elite academic betrayal, maybe, better for logic?

blocks.note: OU is Oxford University, one elite academic body
treason is one kind of betrayal, hence 'maybe'

explanation.surface: Wonders whether a scholar selling out colleagues could ever be justified as more rational.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Better' is a verb meaning to surpass, not an adjective, so the definition is about beating someone in argument.
explanation.definitionFit: To outreason is to surpass someone in reasoning, beating them in argument by the force of sounder thinking.

clue.text: Obtains inside information given rise in savings

indicators.note: the verb for obtains is put inside the word for information
in a down entry, letters that rise read from the bottom upward

blocks.note: gen is British slang for information; it wraps round the verb
obtains = gets

explanation.surface: A trader who obtains insider information sees a rise in their savings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inside information' looks like a single phrase about insider trading, but 'inside' is the instruction and 'information' is the word that holds.
explanation.definitionFit: A nest egg is a sum of money put aside and kept for the future, the idiom coming from an egg left to encourage hens to lay.

clue.text: Welshman, embracing English church, to disappear slowly

indicators.note: to embrace is to hold in the arms, so the Welsh name holds the letter for English

blocks.note: Evans, a very common Welsh surname; its letters wrap round the next piece
E is the abbreviation for English
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A Welsh man hugging the English church before gradually fading away.
explanation.walkthrough: The Welshman is a surname rather than a first name, and the church sits after the embrace, not inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: To evanesce is a literary verb for vanishing gradually, fading like vapour until nothing at all is left.

clue.text: Evil claims a cleaner in church property

indicators.note: to claim something is to take hold of it, so the word for evil takes in the cleaner

blocks.note: vice = evil or wickedness; its letters wrap round the rest
used as itself
a rag is a cloth used for cleaning

explanation.surface: A sinister tale of wickedness claiming a cleaning lady working in a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A cleaner' reads as a person, likely a char, but here it is a humble cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: A vicarage is the house provided for the vicar of a parish, and so it is a building owned by the church.

clue.text: Mad about noisy estate outside fantasy realm

indicators.note: the pieces for about, noisy and estate are placed outside the word for mad

blocks.note: C is circa, Latin for about
noisy = loud
cuckoo is slang for mad
an estate is a piece of land

explanation.surface: Someone raging about a rowdy housing estate, as if it lay beyond the edge of an imaginary kingdom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mad' looks like the definition at the start, but it gives the middle chunk. The name comes from Aristophanes' play The Birds.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names an imaginary, absurdly idealistic place, and is used for any unrealistic dream world of wishful thinking.

clue.text: Boy and girl love workroom

blocks.note: Stu, short for Stuart, a boy's name
Di, short for Diana, a girl's name
love is zero in tennis, which looks like O

explanation.surface: A young couple who love the space where they work together.
explanation.walkthrough: The boy and girl are short forms of names, and 'love' is the tennis score, not a feeling.
explanation.definitionFit: An artist, photographer or broadcaster works in a studio, a room fitted out specifically for creative or technical work.

clue.text: Find nightclub dead

blocks.note: a disco is a nightclub for dancing
dead as an intensifier, as in dead easy, means very

explanation.surface: A grim news report: a body found at a nightclub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Find' is a noun, something found, and 'dead' is the informal adverb meaning extremely, not a corpse.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaeologist's find is their discovery: the thing they came upon or uncovered, both words used as nouns.

clue.text: Fuel can very hot inside

indicators.note: the words for very and hot go inside the word for can

blocks.note: the can is slang for prison, spelt the British way; its letters go round the rest
so = very, as in so hot
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: A warning that a fuel can holds something extremely hot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fuel can' reads as a jerrycan, but 'can' is prison, and gaol is the British spelling of jail.
explanation.definitionFit: Gasohol is petrol blended with ethanol for use in vehicle engines, a mixed motor spirit that burns as a fuel.

clue.text: Whence one cross, in traditional tales, drops from sky

indicators.note: the drops from the sky are put in the word for traditional tales

blocks.note: lore is the body of traditional stories and beliefs; it wraps round the next piece
raindrops fall from the sky

explanation.surface: Tells of a cross, famous in folk tales, falling out of the sky.
explanation.walkthrough: The Cross of Lorraine, with two horizontal bars, was the emblem of the Free French. The definition is cryptic: the region is where one kind of cross comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: Lorraine is a region of north-eastern France that gives its name to a double-barred cross, so one cross comes from there.

clue.text: Company after £500 in shady deal

blocks.note: a monkey is British slang for five hundred pounds
a company is a business

explanation.surface: A firm chasing five hundred pounds by way of a dodgy arrangement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' puts the company second. A monkey for £500 (and a pony for £25) is London slang from betting and the markets.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means underhand trickery or dishonest goings-on, the kind of dodgy scheme that a shady deal involves.

clue.text: One wearing black recalled proud mother

indicators.note: the numeral for one is worn inside the word for black, as clothes surround a wearer
something recalled is called back, so the letters are taken back to front

blocks.note: ebon is a poetic word for black, as in ebony; it goes round the numeral
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Pictures a woman in mourning black remembered for her pride in her children.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is apt: in Greek myth she boasted of her children, the gods killed them all, and she wept endlessly in grief.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek legend she mocked the goddess Leto for having only two offspring and was punished for that boast about her many children.

clue.text: Perhaps wide court passage

blocks.note: in cricket a wide is one kind of extra, a run not scored off the bat
CT is the abbreviation for court

explanation.surface: A legal notice about a corridor in a law court that may or may not be broad.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, a wide is a ball bowled out of the batsman's reach, and the run it gives away is called an extra.
explanation.definitionFit: A passage from a book is a short section quoted or taken from it, which is the same as an extract.

clue.text: Knitted footwear allowing stars to conserve energy

indicators.note: to conserve something is to keep it held in, so the constellation holds the letter for energy

blocks.note: Bootes, the Herdsman, is a northern constellation; its letters go round the next
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Hand-knitted slippers that help celebrities keep warm and save energy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stars' suggests celebrities, but it is a constellation, the one containing the bright star Arcturus.
explanation.definitionFit: Bootees are soft woollen socks or shoes knitted for babies, so they are footwear made on knitting needles.

clue.text: One to examine tickets for theatrical caller?

blocks.note: the official who checks passengers' tickets on a bus or train
the police visitor in J. B. Priestley's 1945 stage play, whose title says he calls

explanation.walkthrough: The second definition needs knowledge of J. B. Priestley's 1945 play An Inspector Calls, a staple of British school syllabuses.
explanation.definitionFit: A ticket checker holds this job title, and the mysterious police visitor in Priestley's stage play is Inspector Goole.

clue.text: Plug firm

blocks.note: a verb: to stop a flow, especially of blood from a wound
an adjective: loyal and steadfast

explanation.walkthrough: The verb is more often spelt stanch, but both spellings are standard for stopping a flow.
explanation.definitionFit: You stem bleeding by pressing on a wound, and a loyal, steadfast supporter who never wavers is also described with this word.

clue.text: Divert sports team approaching course

indicators.note: one thing approaching another comes just before it, so the team is placed in front of the course

blocks.note: a side is a team
a track is a racecourse or path

explanation.surface: A team coach redirected on its way toward a racecourse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Approaching' simply puts the team right before the course.
explanation.definitionFit: To sidetrack someone is to distract them from their main purpose, turning their attention away onto something less important.

clue.text: Openings in colonnade showing dull interior

indicators.note: the colonnade displays the word for dull as its interior, so that word goes inside

blocks.note: a stoa is a Greek covered colonnade; its letters go round the next
mat, or matt, means dull, without shine

explanation.surface: Gaps in a row of columns reveal a drab inside.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as architecture, but the answer is botanical: 'Openings' only looks like the gaps between columns.
explanation.definitionFit: Stomata are the tiny pores on a leaf that let gases pass in and out, and the word is Greek for mouths.

clue.text: Woman, fantastic, needing time to appear earlier

indicators.note: the word for fantastic is rearranged by bringing its letter for time forward one place

blocks.note: great = fantastic, terrific; its final letter is time

explanation.surface: A wonderful woman who needs to arrive sooner.
explanation.walkthrough: The T of the word for fantastic stands for time, and it moves one place toward the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Greta is a female first name, as borne by Greta Garbo, so it serves for any woman in crossword convention.

clue.text: Train ferries coin between terminals in Stoke and Carlisle

indicators.note: a ferry carries passengers inside it, so the outer pieces carry the coin
the coin sits between the two end letters, which therefore enclose it
a terminal is an end of the line, so the last letters of the two stations are used

blocks.note: the final letter of Stoke
a ducat was an old gold coin of Europe
the final letter of Carlisle

explanation.surface: A railway story: a train carrying money between stations at Stoke and Carlisle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Train' reads as the railway noun, but it is a verb meaning teach. Stoke-on-Trent and Carlisle are English towns on the West Coast main line.
explanation.definitionFit: To train someone is to instruct them in a skill, and to educate is to give them teaching or schooling.

clue.text: Energy indeed has missile right out in orbit

indicators.note: the letter for right is out, so it is removed from the missile

blocks.note: E is the physics symbol for energy
indeed! = yes!
a rocket without its R, for right

explanation.surface: A space mission: with plenty of fuel, the missile heads out to the right into orbit.
explanation.walkthrough: The space surface makes 'orbit' look like a path round a planet; here it is the anatomical sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The orbit is the bony cavity in the skull that holds the eyeball, so it is the anatomical name for that hollow.

clue.text: Over there participating in activity on Derwent

indicators.note: the answer takes part in the phrase that follows, sitting inside its letters

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of activity, all of on, and the start of Derwent

explanation.surface: Someone pointing across to people boating on the Derwent.
explanation.walkthrough: The Derwent is a river in the English Lake District and elsewhere. The answer straddles three words.
explanation.definitionFit: Yonder is an old or dialect word pointing to something at a distance but within sight, as in the hills beyond.

clue.text: Dump Beethoven’s Fifth amid unknown music

indicators.note: the fifth letter of the composer's name is the one taken
amid means in the middle of, so the dump and the letter go inside the word for unknown

blocks.note: anon, short for anonymous, of unknown authorship; its letters go round the rest
a tip is a rubbish dump
the fifth letter of Beethoven

explanation.surface: A critic tells us to scrap Beethoven's Fifth Symphony in favour of some obscure piece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beethoven's Fifth' is the famous symphony in the surface, but it means only one letter. 'Unknown' is not X or Y here but anonymous.
explanation.definitionFit: An antiphon is a short chant sung in alternating parts by two choirs, so it is a piece of church music.

clue.text: Hebrew king brought up in island location

indicators.note: in a down entry, something brought up reads from the bottom upward
the upturned king goes inside the word for location

blocks.note: I is the abbreviation for island
a site is a location; its letters go round the king
King Lear, Shakespeare's monarch

explanation.surface: A Hebrew king raised on an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hebrew king' tempts as David or Solomon, but 'Hebrew' alone is the definition and the king is Shakespeare's.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient people of Israel, descendants of Jacob, are called Hebrews, so a member of that nation is one.

clue.text: Sandalwood used for this stretcher?

blocks.note: surface: the fragrant wood from an Indian tree
setter's reading: a sandal is footwear and wood grows on a tree, so the device is footwear plus timber, used to stretch shoes

explanation.walkthrough: Split 'Sandalwood' into its footwear and its timber and you have the device's two halves. A shaped wooden insert keeps a shoe's form and can stretch it.
explanation.definitionFit: The device is a foot-shaped block, often of cedar or beech, pushed into footwear to hold its shape or widen it.

clue.text: Tackle problem resolutely — emulate matador’s hands-on approach?

annotation.answer: TAKE THE BULL BY THE HORNS

blocks.note: the idiom's everyday meaning
a literal reading: a bullfighter who grabs the animal by its head

explanation.walkthrough: The second half reads the idiom literally, with the question mark owning up to the joke; real matadors use a cape, not their hands.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means confronting a difficulty directly and boldly, and literally it is what one would do grappling a charging animal.

clue.text: Bird coming round managed second journey

indicators.note: the bird comes round the other pieces, surrounding them

blocks.note: a tit is a small songbird; its letters go round the rest
ran a business = managed it
S is the abbreviation for second

explanation.surface: A bird returning, having managed a second migration.
explanation.walkthrough: The bird is the small one, not the migrating traveller the surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: Transit is the act of passing or being carried from one place to another, which is what a journey involves.

clue.text: Gander appears with eagle’s wings

blocks.note: she looks tired = she appears tired
the two outside letters of eagle, its wings

explanation.surface: A male goose shows up alongside an eagle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gander' is a male goose in this bird surface, but it is informal British English for a quick glance.
explanation.definitionFit: To take a gander is slang for having a quick glance, and a look-see is a similarly informal word for a brief inspection.

clue.text: One in medical administration’s year with cartel in south-east

indicators.note: the year and cartel are placed in the compass abbreviation for south-east

blocks.note: SE, the compass abbreviation; it wraps round the rest
Y is the abbreviation for year
a ring is a group working together illegally, a cartel

explanation.surface: A health-service manager spends a year with a crime syndicate in the south-east of England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Administration' suggests hospital management, but it is the giving of medicine. The apostrophe-s stands for 'is', linking definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A needle-tipped plunger device is one of the tools a nurse uses when injecting a drug into a patient.

clue.text: Monkey’s mistake, sheltering under tree top

indicators.note: the top of a word is its first letter in a down entry, so only the tree's first letter is used
in a down entry, a word sheltering under another sits directly below it, so it comes second

blocks.note: the first letter of tree
a mistake is an error; in this down entry it sits under the tree's letter

explanation.surface: A monkey slips up while sheltering beneath the top of a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Monkey' is the animal in the surface, but here it means a mischievous child. The apostrophe-s means 'is', and 'sheltering under' places one piece below the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling a naughty child a little monkey or a little terror means the same thing: a mischievous, unruly youngster.

clue.text: Citadel with excellent fencing or one with stronger premises

indicators.note: a fence surrounds what it encloses, so the word for excellent goes round the citadel

blocks.note: A1 means first-class, written with the numeral as I; it goes round the citadel
a citadel is a fort
used as itself
